title: Kunun Gyada
localName: Kunun gyada — groundnut and rice gruel
author: Florence Madu
desc: A hundred and fifty grams of raw groundnut to fifty of rice and six hundred millilitres of water — a cooked gruel, not a fermented drink.
longDesc: Kunun gyada is a light porridge rather than a drink in the kunu family's usual sense, and the important thing to know is that there is no fermentation in it at all — only soaking. Rice soaks at least eight hours, raw groundnuts three, tamarind in warm water until soft. The groundnut milk goes into a pot on medium heat and is stirred constantly to prevent sticking and lumps; when it boils the rice blend is added slowly, and when it boils again the tamarind juice goes in. It is ready once it heats through, and the ratio is unusually clean at three parts groundnut to one of rice.
steps: Soak the rice at least 8 hours.
Soak the tamarind in warm water until soft, then strain out the juice.
Blend the soaked groundnuts with some of the water to a milk, and blend the rice separately.
Pour the groundnut milk into a pot on medium heat, stirring constantly to prevent sticking and lumps.
When it comes to the boil, slowly add the rice blend while stirring.
When it boils again, add the tamarind juice.
Keep stirring until it is heated through. Once it heats up again, it is ready to be served.
chefTips: There is no fermentation here. Only soaking — which makes kunun gyada quite different from kunun zaki despite the shared name.
Stir constantly from the moment the groundnut milk goes in the pot. Groundnut catches and lumps faster than almost anything.
Add the rice blend slowly, into liquid that is already boiling. Dumped in, it seizes.
Three parts groundnut to one part rice, by weight — 150 g to 50 g — in 600 ml of water. A clean, reproducible ratio, which is rare in this part of the record.
Eight hours on the rice and only three on the groundnuts. They do not need the same soak.
Tamarind to taste at the very end. It is the sour note that makes it kunun gyada rather than a groundnut porridge.
Kunu is a category rather than a recipe — kunun gyada is groundnut, kunun aya is tiger nut, kunun zaki is millet or sorghum. They are genuinely different drinks.
commonMistakes: Adding the rice blend to liquid that is not yet boiling.
Soaking the groundnuts as long as the rice.
Adding the tamarind early, where its acidity can curdle the groundnut milk.
sources: Adapted from 'Kunun Gyada (Groundnut Milk and Rice Gruel)', All Nigerian Recipes — no author provided on the page, credited to the site. Headnote as printed: 'Kunun Gyada is a Northern Nigerian gruel (light porridge) made with raw groundnuts and rice.'

Quantities exactly as printed: 150g raw groundnuts (peanuts); 50g soft rice variety; 600 mls cool water; Tamarind (Tsamiya) to taste. That gives GROUNDNUT : RICE : WATER = 150 g : 50 g : 600 ml, a 3:1 solids ratio.

Soaking times as printed: rice 'at least 8 hours'; raw groundnuts '3 hours'; tamarind in warm water until soft. Method as printed: pour the groundnut milk into a pot on medium heat, stirring constantly to prevent sticking and lumps; when boiling, slowly add the rice blend while stirring; when it boils again, add tamarind juice; keep stirring until heated through. DONENESS CUE as printed: 'once it heats up again, it is ready to be served'. Yield not specified.
THERE IS NO FERMENTATION IN THIS RECIPE AT ALL — only soaking. It is a cooked gruel. That matters, because kunu is a family of drinks and several members of it are fermented.

A SECOND, INSTITUTIONAL SOURCE with different ratios: 'Study of traditional Nigerian weaning food based on groundnuts and cereal', authors Iro Nkama, Adamu Iliyas and Amina Jato, United Nations University press archive. Its preparation base is 'partially roasted groundnuts in combination with rice, millet, maize, or sorghum flours; sugar; and tamarind (tsamiya) fruit pulp extract'. Weight ratios of groundnut to cereal as printed: groundnut-rice 57:43; groundnut-millet 41:49; groundnut-maize 51:49; groundnut-sorghum 48:52. Formulations give groundnuts 118–195 g per preparation, sugar 42–53 g, tamarind pulp extract 253–255 ml and water 1,495–1,900 ml. No fermentation times, steeping times or temperatures are specified.

AN ARITHMETIC DEFECT IN THAT PRINTED SOURCE, reproduced rather than corrected: the groundnut-millet ratio is printed as '41:49', which sums to 90 rather than 100, while its other three ratios all sum to 100. It is likely a typo for 41:59 or 51:49, but it is what the paper prints and it is not guessed at here — nor is that ratio used.

DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled: All Nigerian Recipes gives groundnut to rice as 150:50, i.e. 75:25. The UNU study gives groundnut-rice as 57:43. Both are presented as kunun gyada and they are substantially different drinks — the blog version is half again as groundnut-heavy. The blog figures are used above because they are a complete domestic recipe; the UNU ratios are recorded here.

ON THE KUNU FAMILY: 'Just as Kunu refers to milky cream drinks made from cereals (millet, sorghum, rice, groundnuts), so does Horchata mean the milky extract from any vegetable source' — Kitchen Butterfly. So kunu is a category, not a recipe.
FOUR KUNU VARIETIES ARE NOT PUBLISHED IN THIS COLLECTION and the reason is stated at NGA102.
reheating: Low heat with a little water, stirring.
healthBenefits: Groundnut supplies plant protein, niacin and healthy fats.
Tamarind is high in vitamin C and organic acids.
Energy-dense, which is why versions of it are used as weaning food.
culturalNote: Kunun gyada sits between a drink and a meal, and the United Nations University studied versions of it precisely because it is used as a weaning food — groundnut and cereal together give a protein profile neither does alone. The tamarind is not decoration: the acidity is what makes a very rich gruel drinkable.
